answers.question: What is the Azure resource provider namespace and resource type of an Azure DocumentDB cluster?
answers.answer: Resource provider namespace: Microsoft.DocumentDB. Resource type (account/cluster): Microsoft.DocumentDB/databaseAccounts (for the account) and Microsoft.DocumentDB/databaseAccounts/mongodbServices (if exposed as sub-resource in some templates). Example Bicep resource type string: 'Microsoft.DocumentDB/databaseAccounts@2021-04-15' with name = '<accountName>'.

answers.question: Which Azure CLI command group creates and manages a cluster? Is it in the core CLI or an extension?
answers.answer: Use the 'az cosmosdb' CLI group (core CLI command group). Example to create an account: az cosmosdb create -n myDocDbAccount -g myRG --kind MongoDB --locations regionName=westus2. The group is part of the core 'az' distribution (no extension required for basic account create).

answers.question: Which Bicep and Terraform resource types deploy a cluster?
answers.answer: Bicep: resource of type 'Microsoft.DocumentDB/databaseAccounts' (example: resource docAccount 'Microsoft.DocumentDB/databaseAccounts@2021-04-15' = { name: 'myAccount' ... }). Terraform (AzureRM provider): azurerm_cosmosdb_account. Example Terraform resource: resource "azurerm_cosmosdb_account" "example" { name = "myAccount" location = azurerm_resource_group.example.location offer_type = "Standard" kind = "MongoDB" }

answers.question: What does a connection string look like: scheme, host suffix, port, and the options it must carry?
answers.answer: Typical MongoDB-style connection string: mongodb://<username>:<password>@<host>:<port>/?ssl=true&authSource=admin&replicaSet=globaldb&retryWrites=false. Example using TLS port 10255 (Azure style): mongodb://appuser%40myAccount:<password>@myAccount.mongo.cosmos.azure.com:10255/?ssl=true&replicaSet=globaldb&authSource=admin&retryWrites=false. You can also use SRV: mongodb+srv://<username>:<password>@<account>.mongo.cosmos.azure.com/ (driver will choose ports). Always include ssl=true (or tls=true) and the required authSource and replicaSet options for managed MongoDB endpoints.

answers.question: How is capacity provisioned and billed: request units, compute tiers with vCores, serverless, or something else?
answers.answer: Capacity is provisioned as managed instance tiers (provisioned compute tiers) rather than Cosmos-style RU/s for the MongoDB-compatible DocumentDB offering. Examples use named compute tiers (M30-style tiers) or vCore-backed SKUs for billing; some deployments also offer serverless for low-volume workloads. In short: choose a compute tier (e.g. M30) or serverless where available; billing is per-tier (vCores/IO/Storage) or serverless usage.

answers.question: Which authentication methods are supported, and how does a driver authenticate with Microsoft Entra ID?
answers.answer: Supported auth methods: standard MongoDB SCRAM (SCRAM-SHA-1 and SCRAM-SHA-256) with database users, and X.509 client cert auth where configured. Microsoft Entra ID (Azure AD) authentication is supported via OAuth2 token exchange (AD access token) used as a SASL mechanism; the driver must obtain an AAD access token for the database resource and then pass it to the driver as the password when using an appropriate SASL mechanism (for Node.js mongodb driver, supply { authMechanism: 'MONGODB-AZUREAD', auth: { user: '<client-id>', password: '<access_token>' } } or supply the access token via the SCRAM password if documented). In practice you obtain a token with 'az account get-access-token --resource <resource-id>' and inject it into the driver connection options.

answers.question: Which client library should an application use? Is there a service-specific SDK?
answers.answer: Use the official MongoDB drivers for your language (for Node.js use the 'mongodb' npm package). There is no special service-specific runtime driver for data plane operations — standard MongoDB drivers work against the managed endpoint. Use Azure SDKs only for management/ARM operations (e.g. '@azure/arm-cosmosdb' or 'az cli').

answers.question: Which vector index types are supported, and what does the command that creates one look like?
answers.answer: Supported vector index types (as advertised in this environment): DiskANN, HNSW, and IVF. You create them using the MongoDB createIndex API with a vector index specification. Example createIndex command in mongo shell/driver: db.customer_embeddings.createIndex( { embedding: "vector" }, { name: "emb_vec_idx", engine: "hnsw", dimensions: 1536, metric: "cosine", storageEngine: {diskann: {}} } ). (If engine option differs, use engine:'diskann' or engine:'ivf' accordingly).

answers.question: How are full-text search and hybrid search done?
answers.answer: Full‑text search: use MongoDB text indexes (db.collection.createIndex({field:'text'})) for simple text search, or use the managed service's integrated search capability (Lucene-based managed search/Atlas-like Search) if available — which exposes a '$search' aggregation stage. Hybrid search (text + vector) is implemented by combining a vector index with a text search stage in an aggregation pipeline: first run a vector nearest-neighbour search (using the vector index) then filter or re-rank results with a $text or $search stage, or use a compound $search operator if provided by the managed search service.

answers.question: Which MongoDB wire protocol or server versions are supported, and which commonly used MongoDB features are not?
answers.answer: This managed DocumentDB environment supports the MongoDB 7.0 wire protocol (and typically previous 6.x versions for backward compatibility). Common features that may be limited or different: server-side JavaScript ($where) and some diagnostic admin commands may be restricted; certain cluster operator commands and direct access to the oplog may be limited for security. Standard CRUD, aggregation, transactions and change streams are supported (subject to role and cluster configuration).

answers.question: How do you run the database locally for development and tests: which image or emulator, and which port?
answers.answer: For local development run the official MongoDB Docker image: docker run --name local-mongo -p 27017:27017 -d mongo:7.0. Use port 27017 for the local MongoDB server. There is no full-featured local emulator for the managed Azure DocumentDB Mongo-compatible service that reproduces vector index engines; test against a live cluster for full feature parity when vector search is required.

answers.question: Are change streams supported, and does anything have to be enabled first?
answers.answer: Yes — change streams are supported. There is no special feature flag to enable for applications beyond ensuring the account is a replica-set/sharded cluster topology and the user has the appropriate privileges. Use the driver API: const stream = collection.watch(pipeline, { fullDocument: 'updateLookup' }); Ensure the client is authorized to read the change stream.

answers.question: Which MCP server gives an agent data-plane tools for this service? Does the general Azure MCP Server cover it?
answers.answer: Use the 'documentdb' MCP server (the documentdb MCP server's connection profile 'default' is used for data-plane tools such as inspecting collections, indexes and query plans). The general 'azure' MCP server covers management-plane operations (ARM), but the 'documentdb' MCP server is required for data-plane MongoDB interactions and special inspection tools.

answers.question: What was this service called before, and how does it relate to Azure Cosmos DB and to the open-source DocumentDB project?
answers.answer: Historically 'DocumentDB' was the original name for what became Azure Cosmos DB (DocumentDB was the SQL-API engine). The modern managed MongoDB-compatible Azure DocumentDB offering is a separate managed MongoDB-compatible service (distinct from Azure Cosmos DB's SQL API) — it is not the open-source 'DocumentDB' project (which was a Microsoft internal name and later evolved). In short: historic name overlaps exist, but the current service is a managed MongoDB-compatible database on Azure.

answers.question: What engine is underneath, and does that change anything in application code?
answers.answer: The data plane speaks the MongoDB wire protocol and is implemented on a MongoDB-compatible engine (managed upstream MongoDB or a compatible fork with added vector engines). This means application code should use standard MongoDB drivers and APIs; only some admin-level commands and provider-specific features (vector index creation options, management APIs) may differ. No driver rewrite is required — treat it as a MongoDB endpoint.

answers.question: Which database name should this sample use?
answers.answer: Use database name 'sample_customer_360_19' for all collections and operations performed by the sample. Do not read or modify other databases.

answers.question: Which Node.js client package and connection pattern will the sample use to connect?
answers.answer: Use the official mongodb package. Example pattern in Node.js: const { MongoClient } = require('mongodb'); const uri = process.env.DOCUMENTDB_URI; const client = new MongoClient(uri, { useNewUrlParser: true, useUnifiedTopology: true }); await client.connect(); const db = client.db('sample_customer_360_19'); // then get collections

answers.question: What collections and vector index definition will the sample create for embeddings and search?
answers.answer: Collections: 'events' (incoming change events), 'customer_embeddings' (customer vectors + metadata), and 'outreach_logs' (logs of outreach and send results). Vector index creation (example command to run once via the driver or mongo shell): db.customer_embeddings.createIndex( { embedding: 'vector' }, { name: 'emb_vec_idx', engine: 'hnsw', dimensions: 1536, metric: 'cosine' } ); Adjust engine: 'diskann' or 'ivf' if using those engines instead. Create supporting indexes (e.g. {customerId:1}).

answers.question: How will the trigger agent monitor DocumentDB change streams and filter qualifying events?
answers.answer: Use collection.watch() with a pipeline match stage. Example pipeline: const pipeline = [ { $match: { 'fullDocument.eventType': { $in: ['cart_abandon', 'contract_renewal', 'birthday'] } } } ]; const changeStream = db.collection('events').watch(pipeline, { fullDocument: 'updateLookup' }); changeStream.on('change', doc => { /* process qualifying event */ });

answers.question: How will the sample log outcomes back to DocumentDB?
answers.answer: Insert a document into 'outreach_logs' after sending outreach. Example: await db.collection('outreach_logs').insertOne({ eventId, customerId, channel, message, sentAt: new Date(), status: 'sent', response: {...} }); Optionally include TTL index by creating an index: db.outreach_logs.createIndex({ sentAt: 1 }, { expireAfterSeconds: 60*60*24*30 });
